"Se anunció" is the impersonal "se", where English uses the passive "was announced". The doer is not named because it does not matter.
"Un martes" with the indefinite article means "one Tuesday, some Tuesday". With "el martes" it would be a specific one, and the whole joke depends on that "un".
"Que es cuando" is a relative clause referring to the whole preceding idea. "Nunca" before the verb needs no extra "no", and "nada bueno" places the adjective after the pronoun.
"Nos prometieron" is a subjectless plural verb. Spanish cannot make the person the subject of a passive here, so the English "we were promised" has to be recast.
"Menos niveles" uses one word for both countable and uncountable, so the English split between "fewer" and "less" has no equivalent.
"Decisiones más rápidas" builds the comparative with "más" and places it after the noun, along with the adjective. English puts both before.
"Seis meses después" needs no preposition, and "después" follows the period.
"Ambas cosas" is more formal than "las dos". Note that "ambas" needs no article, unlike "las dos".
"Y además" adds with a slight shift. "Dos comités nuevos" puts the adjective after the noun; before it, "nuevos comités", it would mean "further ones".
"Mi propio puesto" doubles the possessive for emphasis. "Propio" agrees with the noun and must follow the possessive, never replace it.
The present perfect for something whose result still holds. "Formalmente" means "officially", and the adverb comes after the participle.

"Cosa que" refers back to the whole clause, and it is a slightly more colloquial alternative to "lo cual". "Terminar de" plus the infinitive means "to quite do something", which is exactly the shade English gets from "quite".
"Depender de" always takes "de", and it is the standard verb for reporting to someone.
"De alguien" carries the "de" demanded by the verb. "Alguien" is invariable.

"Que depende de" repeats the verb and its preposition. "Mi anterior jefa" puts "anterior" before the noun, where it means "previous"; after it, the sense would be closer to "the one before in a list".
"Para ser justos" is a fixed parenthetical phrase using the infinitive.
"Ella es muy buena" adds the pronoun for contrast, which Spanish does only deliberately. "Ser" is used because it is a lasting quality.
"Más cortas" agrees in the feminine plural with "reuniones". "Ser" again, because it is presented as how things now are.
"Si" introduces a noun clause acting as the subject, not a condition. This "si" carries no accent.
"Contar como" takes "as" in English and "como" here. The phrase repeats the wording from the second line, and the repetition is deliberate.
"Depende de cómo se cuente" uses the subjunctive after "cómo" because the manner is left open. The accent on "cómo" survives inside the indirect question.
"Lo más difícil" uses the neuter article with a superlative, "the hardest thing". Spanish needs no word for "thing".
"De hablar" carries the "de" demanded by "lo más difícil". "Bien" goes between the verb and its object, which Spanish allows and English does not.
"Dejar de" plus the infinitive means "to stop doing". "Hacerte concesiones" attaches the pronoun to the infinitive.
"En el B1" keeps the article before the level, unlike English "at B1".
"Emocionarse de" is reflexive and takes "de" before the clause. "Todos" is plural and takes a plural verb, unlike English "everyone".
"De que supiera" requires the subjunctive, because the emotion is a reaction rather than a report. "Un café" with the article means one cup, as opposed to uncountable coffee.
"En algún punto después" uses "punto" for a point in time. "Algún" is the shortened form before a masculine noun.
"Se acabaron" is reflexive and puts the verb before the subject, which Spanish does to introduce something new.
"Empezaron las correcciones" repeats that word order for symmetry. The parallel is what produces the effect.
"Eso es progreso" leaves "progreso" without an article, which Spanish does when the noun is a bare predicate.
"Aunque ... lo parezca" takes the subjunctive because the concession is being conceded rather than stated. "Lo" is the neuter pronoun standing for the whole idea.
"En el momento" keeps the article and means "at the time". Without it, "en momentos", the sense would change entirely.
"El último diez por ciento" keeps the article before "último", and the verb that follows is singular.
"No es vocabulario" negates the copula and opens the "no ... sino ..." frame.
"Sino" closes the frame and cannot be replaced by "pero". "Saber cuándo no pasarse de listo" chains an infinitive, an indirect question and a negated reflexive infinitive.
"Pasarse" is reflexive and means "to overdo it". "Todavía" goes before the verb.
"Con una palabra" uses "con" for the means.
The relative "que" cannot be dropped, unlike English "that". "Esa misma mañana" places "misma" after the demonstrative for emphasis.
"La fluidez" keeps the article, as any subject noun does.
"Por lo que voy viendo" is a fixed parenthetical phrase using "ir" plus a gerund, which conveys a gradual process English would render with "as far as I can tell".
"Contención" needs no article as a bare predicate. "Sobre todo" softens the claim.
"Ya he pasado" pairs the present perfect with "ya". In Spain this tense is the natural choice for a count that reaches into the present.
"Más horas ... que" has its "que" further on. "Esa oficina de Hacienda" uses a demonstrative and links the nouns with "de"; "Hacienda" is capitalised as the name of the institution.
"En casa de" is the fixed way to say "at somebody's home", and Spanish has no possessive apostrophe to do it with. "La mayoría de" takes "de".
"Cada visita" takes a singular noun, as "cada" always does.
"Exigir" is stronger than "necesitar" and fits the bureaucratic tone.
"Solo" as an adverb takes no accent. "Después de" needs both words, and "la visita anterior" puts the adjective after the noun.
"La señora de la ventanilla cuatro" links the nouns with "de", and the number follows the noun with no article, as in "la habitación cinco".
The present perfect "ha desarrollado", for something that has taken shape and still holds.
"Cierta simpatía" without an article means "a certain amount of". With "una cierta" it would sound heavier and slightly odd here. "Simpatía por" takes "por".
"Ya no" together means "no longer". "Me pregunta" puts the pronoun before the verb.
"A qué vengo" keeps the "a" demanded by "venir a", and the accent on "qué" survives in the indirect question.
The semicolon joins two independent clauses. "Alargar la mano hacia" is the natural phrase where English says "reach for".
"La semana pasada" keeps the article and takes no preposition.
"Me dijo" puts the indirect object pronoun before the verb.
"Ya casi había terminado" uses the pluperfect, because the finishing is set before the moment of speaking. "Ya casi" stacks two adverbs, which is idiomatic.
"Eso ya lo había oído antes" doubles the object: "eso" is fronted and "lo" repeats it. Spanish requires that doubling whenever the object comes first.
The present perfect again in "he aprendido", with the auxiliary repeated. Spanish repeats it more readily than English does.
"Aprender a" takes "a", and the negation goes before the infinitive: "a no celebrarlo".
"Aun así" means "even so", and "aun" here carries no accent.
"Algo curiosamente reconfortante" places the adjective after "algo", as Spanish always does with this pronoun.
"Te reconoce la cara" uses the article where English uses a possessive: Spanish marks the owner with the pronoun "te" instead.
"El mejor jefe que he tenido" combines a superlative with a relative clause, and "que" cannot be dropped.
"No decía casi nada" needs both "no" and "nada", the double negation Spanish requires and English forbids.
"En las reuniones" keeps the article, where English says "in meetings" with none.
The imperfect "dejaba" describes a repeated habit, which is how Spanish renders the English "would let".
"Los ruidosos" is an adjective used as a noun with the article, "the loud ones".
After "dejar que" the verb goes into the subjunctive: "terminaran". English uses a bare infinitive after "let", so this construction has to be rebuilt from scratch.
"Luego hacía" keeps the imperfect for the same repeated habit. "Hacer una pregunta" is the collocation, not "preguntar una pregunta".
"Una pregunta" with the indefinite article, and "una" here carries the sense of "a single one".
"Que recolocaba la sala" opens a relative clause in the imperfect. "Sin ruido" is a noun phrase where English uses the adverb "quietly".
"Tardar años" means "to take years", with the person as the subject. English says "it took me years", with an impersonal "it".
"Tardar en" plus the infinitive needs "en". "Darme cuenta" attaches the pronoun to the infinitive.
"De que" carries the "de" demanded by "darse cuenta". "Aquello" is the far demonstrative, which distances the memory.
"Lo he intentado" uses the neuter "lo" for the whole approach, with the present perfect.
"Unas cuatro veces" uses "unas" for approximation — the feminine plural of "uno" agreeing with "veces".
"En tres ocasiones" takes "en", where English uses "on".
"La cuarta" drops the noun "vez", which is understood, and keeps the feminine agreement.
"Demasiado pronto" places "demasiado" before the adverb, and it stays invariable there.
"Sonó maleducado" uses an adjective after a linking verb, agreeing with the implied masculine subject. "Simplemente" softens it.
"El momento oportuno" places the adjective after the noun. Spanish has no single word for "timing".
"Por lo visto" is a fixed parenthetical phrase, "apparently".
"Lo único que nadie puede enseñarte" uses the neuter "lo" with an adjective, and "nadie" after the verb needs no extra "no" because the clause already begins negatively enough with "que".
"Mi madre" uses a possessive instead of an article.
"Empezar a" keeps its compulsory "a", and "contarme" attaches the pronoun to the infinitive.
"Que ya me sé" uses "saberse" reflexively, which adds the sense of knowing something by heart. Plain "sé" would be flatter.
"Durante un tiempo" uses "durante" for the duration.
"La corregía" is the imperfect for a repeated action, with the object pronoun before the verb.
"Lo cual" refers back to the whole clause, and "no ayudaba a nadie" carries the double negation Spanish demands.
"Ahora escucho" opens the contrast with the past.
The gerund "buscando" expresses purpose, where English uses the preposition in "listen for".
"Siempre las hay" uses the impersonal "hay" with an object pronoun in front — an unusual-looking combination that is perfectly standard.
"La versión que contó" needs its "que". "La primavera pasada" keeps the article and takes no preposition.
"Un final distinto" places the adjective after the noun.
"Distinto del que" takes "de", and "el que" is the relative with an article, agreeing with "final". "De niño" means "as a child", with no article at all.
The present perfect "he decidido", for a decision that still stands.
"Las dos" keeps the article, unlike "ambas" in the first phrase. "Ciertas" agrees in the feminine plural.
"En el sentido que importa" uses "que" as the subject of its clause, where it cannot be dropped.
"No está perdiendo" is the present continuous with "estar", used here precisely because the process is unfinished.
"Seguir" plus a gerund means "to still be doing". The subject is left unsaid, and the semicolon marks the turn.
"Lo que significa" uses the neuter "lo que" for a whole idea.
"Sospechar" opens the clause with "que", which is compulsory.
"Dentro de unos treinta años" is the fixed way to say "in about thirty years", with "unos" doing the approximating.
"Estaré haciendo" is the future continuous with "estar". "Exactamente lo mismo" uses the neuter "lo" with "mismo".
"La caída" is the ordinary word for an outage. "Durar" is intransitive.
"Once minutos" is a duration complement with no preposition.
"Vamos a comentar" uses "ir a" for the future, and "durante once meses" gives the span. The contrast between minutes and months is the joke.
"La causa" keeps the article as a subject noun.
"Un cambio de configuración" links the nouns with "de", where English simply puts them side by side.
"Recordar haber aprobado" uses a perfect infinitive after the verb — a compact construction with no English equivalent, since English would say "remembers approving".
"El post mortem" is a Latin borrowing kept in two words, and it takes the masculine article.
The quoted phrase goes in angle quotes. "Sin culpables" uses "sin" plus a bare plural noun.
"En el sentido de que" needs both "de" and "que". "De quién era" keeps the accent on "quién" inside the indirect question.
"Redactar" is the precise verb for drawing up a document, more exact than "hacer".
"Puntos de acción" links the nouns with "de".
"De los cuales" places the preposition before the relative, which agrees in gender and number. "Los dos fáciles" drops the noun but keeps the article.
"En nuestro descargo" is a fixed legal-sounding phrase, "in our defence".
"Los otros doce" keeps the article before "otros" when speaking of the remainder of a known set.
"Habrían exigido" is the compound conditional for something that did not happen. "Admitir algo estructural" places the adjective after "algo".
"El sistema" is masculine despite the "-a" ending, like "el tema" and "el problema".
"Un poco más seguro" stacks a softener with the comparative.
"Bastante más complicado" mirrors the previous element with a stronger intensifier. The symmetry is deliberate.
"Yo diría que eso" adds the pronoun for emphasis and uses the conditional to soften.
"Una descripción honesta" places the adjective after the noun.
"De casi toda la ingeniería" keeps the article after "toda", which is compulsory.
"Antes" plus the imperfect is how Spanish says "used to". There is no separate construction, and the tense carries all of it.
"Todos los libros" keeps the article after "todos". The relative "que" is compulsory.
"Por principio" uses "por" for the motive and takes no article.
"El principio" keeps the article, referring back to what was just named.
"Resultar ser" needs the infinitive "ser" after it.
"Vanidad" needs no article as a bare predicate. "Sobre todo" softens the claim.
"Los abandono" places the object pronoun before the verb.
"Sin remordimiento" uses "sin" plus a bare singular noun, where the plural would also be possible but heavier.
"Bastante más" intensifies a comparative that modifies the verb rather than an adjective.
"Hay un placer particular" uses the invariable "hay". "Particular" after the noun means "special".
"En cerrar" takes an infinitive after the preposition, where English uses the "-ing" form.
"Que se suponía que debías admirar" stacks two "que" and an impersonal "se". Spanish cannot drop either conjunction, so the sentence keeps a shape English would trim away.
"El mismo placer que" takes "que" after "el mismo", not "como". This is a genuine trap for English speakers, whose "the same as" points the other way.
"Irse de una fiesta" is reflexive and takes "de". The infinitive matches the one in the previous element.
"En el momento exacto" places the adjective after the noun.
"Mis estanterías" uses the plural possessive, which changes only for number.
"Quedar" plus an adjective means "to end up", and "menos impresionantes" builds the comparison downwards.
"Mucho más honestas" mirrors the previous element and agrees in the feminine plural. The symmetry is intentional.
"Nadie viene" places the negative pronoun before the verb, so no extra "no" is needed.
"A preguntar por ellas" uses "a" for the purpose and "por" for the topic. "Preguntar por" means asking about something, while "preguntar a" would mean asking a person.
"Que era justo lo que yo temía" refers back to the whole clause. "Justo" here means "exactly", and the pronoun "yo" is added for emphasis.
"Ponerse a" plus the infinitive means "to take up doing", and the reflexive pronoun is part of it.
"A una edad" uses "a" for the age.
"En la que" places the preposition before the relative, which careful Spanish requires. "Ponerse a" repeats from the first element, and that repetition is the joke.
"El primer mes" uses the shortened "primer" before a masculine noun.
"Fue humillante" uses the preterite of "ser" for a closed period, with the present participle as an adjective.
"De una manera que había olvidado que existía" nests two relative clauses, each with its own "que". Neither can be dropped.
"Los adultos" keeps the article for a general statement.
"No solemos ser" uses "soler" in the first person plural, which quietly includes the speaker in the group. English would need a separate sentence to do that.
"Malos en algo" uses "en", not "de". "Delante de otros" is the natural equivalent of English "in public" here.
"Hay un monitor" uses the invariable "hay". "Monitor" is the word for a sports instructor.
"Llevar desde marzo viéndome" combines "llevar" plus a gerund with a starting point, and the pronoun attaches to the gerund. The whole thing sits in the present, where English needs a perfect.
"No respirar correctamente" is a negated infinitive depending on "viéndome". The negation goes before the infinitive.
"Nunca ha insinuado" places "nunca" before the verb, so no second negative is required there.
"Ni una sola vez" reinforces the negation already present. Two negative expressions in one clause are normal in Spanish and impossible in English.
"Que quizá sea" takes the subjunctive after "quizá", because the suggestion is hypothetical. "Mayor para esto" uses "para" for the purpose.
"Esa contención" uses a demonstrative instead of an article.
"Vale más para mí" uses "valer" with "para" for the person.
"Que la propia técnica" takes "que" after the comparative, and "propia" before the noun means "the technique itself".
"Ahora soy lento" uses "ser" for a lasting characteristic rather than "estar".
"En una distancia mucho más larga" stacks an intensifier with the comparative.
"Llamar a eso progreso" needs the "a" before "eso" and leaves "progreso" without an article. The present perfect marks it as a decision that stands.
"La mitad de mi trabajo" takes "de" before the possessive, and the verb after "la mitad" is singular.
"Consistir en" always takes "en". "Decirle a la gente" doubles the indirect object: the pronoun "le" and the named person both appear, which Spanish requires.
"Que ya sabe" agrees with "la gente" in the singular, even though it means many people.
"La otra mitad" keeps the article before "otra".
"Es ser" puts an infinitive after the copula. It looks odd and is entirely correct.
"A la que se le permite" combines a relative with a preposition, an impersonal "se" and a doubled indirect object "le". Spanish stacks all three without strain.
"Nadie paga" places the negative pronoun before the verb.
"Por el análisis" uses "por" for what is paid for, and keeps the article.
The semicolon joins the contrast. "Pagan" is a subjectless plural, and that shift alone carries the point.
"Sonar" is a linking verb, so "cínico" is an adjective, agreeing with the implied masculine subject.
"Durante casi un año" uses "durante" for the span and "casi" for the approximation.
"Hacer sentir" is a causative construction with two verbs in a row. "Fatal" is an adverb here, and it is invariable.
"Darse cuenta" is reflexive, and the preterite marks the moment of realising.
"De que" carries the "de" demanded by "darse cuenta". "De verdad" goes after the verb.
"Más de lo que consigue" uses "de lo que" before a clause, never "que". "La mayoría de los informes" takes a singular verb.
"Dejar de fingir" chains two verbs with the compulsory "de".
"El valor" keeps its article as the subject of the clause.
"Está en las diapositivas" uses "estar" for location, which is the only correct choice here.
"Está en la sala" repeats the same verb, with the subject left unsaid.
"Y las diapositivas" keeps the article, as any subject noun does.
"Lo que hacemos con las manos" uses the neuter "lo que" and the article where English uses a possessive: "con las manos", not "con nuestras manos".
"Hace poco" means "recently", built on the impersonal "hacer". "Me preguntaron" is a subjectless plural.
"Qué me diría a mí mismo" keeps the accent on "qué" and doubles the pronoun: "me" and "a mí mismo" both appear, which is how Spanish gives emphasis.
"A los veinticinco" uses "a los" for the age, and the article is part of the construction.
"La respuesta honesta" places the adjective after the noun.
"No me habría hecho caso" uses the compound conditional for something that did not happen. "Hacer caso" is a fixed phrase, and it takes an indirect object.
"Habría hecho bien" keeps the compound conditional and drops the subject, which is understood.
"Casi todo lo que sé ahora" uses the neuter "lo que" after "todo".
"Lo sé porque ignoré" doubles the object with "lo", because the fronted "todo lo que sé" is repeated by the pronoun. Spanish requires that doubling.
"Ese tipo de consejos" links the nouns with "de", and "justamente" intensifies the demonstrative.
"Los errores" keeps the article for a general statement.
"No fueron desvíos" uses the preterite for a closed judgement.
"Eran el camino" switches to the imperfect, and the switch is the point: the preterite closed the first half, the imperfect opens the mistakes out into something that lasted.
"Dicho esto" is an absolute participle construction, "that said".
"Probablemente sí mencionaría" uses "sí" as an emphatic particle, not as "yes". It has no English equivalent and simply strengthens the verb.
"Lo del sueño" uses the neuter article with "de", meaning "the thing about sleep". It is a compact construction Spanish uses constantly.
"Se habría reído" is the compound conditional of a reflexive verb, with the pronoun before the auxiliary.
"Habría tomado nota" repeats the auxiliary, which Spanish does more readily than English. "Tomar nota" takes no article.
"Lo habría olvidado para el jueves" uses "para" for a deadline, and "lo" for the whole matter.
"Que es, más o menos" begins the sentence with a relative referring to everything before it, with the parenthetical set off by commas.
"Lo que hice yo" places the pronoun after the verb for emphasis, which Spanish can do freely.
"Con todo lo que me dijeron" ends with a subjectless plural verb, where English used the passive "I was told".
